title: Ansel and the Summer
premise: Marine biologist Vesper Ashgrove has spent eleven years in the coastal town of Saltmere counting sea turtles and avoiding Ansel Reyes, the boy she loved and abandoned after a fire took her family's inn and her courage with it. When a renovation crew uncovers an unsent letter she wrote him at seventeen, postmarked the summer everything ended, Ansel returns to town to finally ask why. As they restore the ruined inn together, Vesper learns the letter was never lost—Ansel's late mother kept it all these years—and that his own inheritance of grief mirrors hers. When the last train of the season leaves and Ansel must choose between a job abroad and staying, Vesper finally lets someone stay: she asks him to, out loud, and they rebuild the inn as theirs.
about_author: Paloma Kavanagh is a former tide-pool docent who writes love stories set in small coastal towns where everyone knows your business and forgives you anyway. She lives on a windswept peninsula with her partner, two rescue dogs, and an unreasonable number of shells.

chapters.title: The Count
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. During the annual turtle census, Vesper catalogs nests with practiced detachment, revealing her habit of replacing feeling with data. A demolition crew at her family's derelict inn unearths a weathered letter addressed to Ansel Reyes. Emotional beat: dread disguised as curiosity—the past has been physically uncovered.

chapters.title: Postmarked Eleven Years Ago
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. She reads her own teenage letter—raw, hopeful, never sent—and burns to destroy it but cannot. Her aunt reveals the crew found it sealed behind a wall. That night, word spreads that Ansel is coming back for the summer season. Emotional beat: panic; the life she built on avoidance begins cracking.

chapters.title: The Man Off the Last Train
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. He arrives carrying his mother's ashes and a box of her belongings—including, he doesn't yet know, the letter's twin: Vesper's reply to a note he never received. He takes a room above the hardware store and tells himself it's only for the estate sale. Emotional beat: guarded hope mistaken for indifference.

chapters.title: Salt and Small Talk
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Vesper and Ansel collide at the diner, performing civility while eleven years hum beneath every sentence. They agree, stiffly, to split proceeds from the inn's sale by restoring it first. Emotional beat: the first honest laugh, which frightens them both more than anger would.

chapters.title: What the Walls Kept
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Stripping wallpaper, Ansel finds scorch marks from the fire and his mother's handwriting on a beam—a message to whoever renovated next. He realizes she knew about the letter, about Vesper, about everything. Emotional beat: grief reframed; his mother was a keeper of other people's chances.

chapters.title: Nesting Season
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. A storm threatens a turtle nest and Ansel shows up at midnight to help her relocate eggs, working shoulder to shoulder in the rain. Afterwards, soaked and laughing in her truck, the old intimacy flickers. Emotional beat: desire resurfacing alongside terror of repeating old wounds.

chapters.title: The Reply She Never Sent
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. Sorting his mother's box, Ansel finds Vesper's unsent reply to his own long-lost note—proof they both tried once and were failed by timing and fear. Furious and heartbroken, he confronts Vesper mid-restoration. Emotional beat: climax of resentment; the truth that neither abandoned the other by choice.

chapters.title: Low Tide
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV. Devastated that their second chance nearly drowned twice, Vesper walks the flats at low tide and finally grieves her family, the fire, and her decade of hiding. She drafts a new letter—one she intends to deliver by hand. Emotional beat: surrender; choosing vulnerability over invisibility.

chapters.title: After the Last Train Leaves
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The final train of the season departs without Ansel—but not because he stayed for the inn. Vesper finds him on the empty platform and, voice shaking, asks him to stay. He gives her his mother's letter and says yes before she finishes. Emotional beat: the climactic ask; love chosen aloud at last.

chapters.title: Ansel and the Summer
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV, epilogue-adjacent. Weeks later, the inn reopens under both their names; the hatchlings make their run to the sea as guests watch. Vesper mails nothing ever again—she says things out loud now. Final image: two names painted on the sign, the tide coming in. Emotional beat: belonging earned, inheritance transformed into home.
